children.text: How Anxiety Can Affect Daily Functioning

Anxiety can affect daily functioning by making it harder to care for yourself, complete responsibilities, make decisions, travel, attend appointments, work, study, maintain relationships, and participate independently in ordinary activities.

The impact may be obvious, such as missing work because of panic attacks. It may also be less visible, such as completing responsibilities only through hours of checking, reassurance seeking, overpreparation, physical tension, and exhaustion.
Anxiety-related functional impairment may include difficulty with:
Getting out of bed and beginning the day

Anxiety disorders can interfere with routine activities, including job performance, schoolwork, relationships, and household responsibilities. Functional impairment is one of the important differences between temporary nervousness and a possible anxiety disorder.

A person does not need to lose all ability to function before anxiety deserves professional attention. Someone may remain employed, attend school, care for a family, or appear confident while experiencing significant distress and limitation.
This page focuses specifically on functional impairment. For a broader discussion of how anxiety influences routines, choices, health behaviors, and relationships, visit
Daily functioning refers to a person’s ability to complete necessary and meaningful activities.

Mental health professionals may evaluate functioning across several areas rather than looking only at symptom intensity. Common areas include communication, mobility, self-care, relationships, household activities, work or school, and participation in the community.
A person may function well in one area while experiencing major difficulty in another.
Someone may perform well at work but be unable to drive.
A student may earn good grades but avoid all social contact.
A parent may care for children but neglect their own medical needs.
A person may maintain hygiene but remain unable to leave home alone.
The clinician should consider the complete pattern.
How Does Anxiety Interfere With Functioning?
Anxiety may interfere through several connected mechanisms.
Worry can consume attention that would otherwise be used for work, conversations, planning, memory, and problem-solving.
Rapid heartbeat, muscle tension, nausea, trembling, sweating, dizziness, or shortness of breath may make ordinary activities feel unsafe.
The person may avoid situations associated with anxiety, panic, embarrassment, uncertainty, or uncomfortable physical sensations.
Repeatedly asking others for confirmation may delay decisions and reduce independent confidence.
The person may repeatedly check work, locks, health information, messages, schedules, or completed tasks.
Fear of mistakes may cause overpreparation, procrastination, missed deadlines, or inability to complete tasks.
Anxiety-related insomnia may reduce concentration, judgment, emotional regulation, and physical energy.
Fear of another panic attack may lead the person to avoid driving, travel, crowds, exercise, or being alone.
These patterns can reinforce one another.
A person feels anxious about driving.
They become less confident in their ability to drive.
They depend increasingly on another person.
Work, appointments, and independence become restricted.
Functional Impairment May Be Visible or Hidden
Spending hours preparing for a routine meeting
Arriving extremely early because of fear
Calling family members throughout the day for reassurance
Using alcohol to tolerate social situations
Working late because nothing feels complete
Recovering for hours after an ordinary interaction
Avoiding promotions or relationships without explaining why
A person can appear productive while functioning at an unsustainable emotional and physical cost.
The appropriate question is not only:
“What did completing it require, and what other parts of life were affected?”
Anxiety may interfere with morning functioning before a person gets out of bed.
The person may wake thinking about:
Leaving home much earlier than necessary
A morning routine may become increasingly complicated as the person adds checking and preparation intended to prevent anxiety.
Anxiety can affect bathing, grooming, dental care, dressing, and other personal-care activities.
A person may avoid hygiene because of:
Fear of fainting in the shower
Another person may spend excessive time:
Preparing to be seen by others

Not every repeated hygiene behavior is caused by an anxiety disorder. Obsessive-compulsive symptoms, trauma, depression, body-image concerns, sensory issues, and medical conditions may require consideration.
A major decline in hygiene may indicate worsening mental health and should be discussed with a professional.
Anxiety may interfere with eating through:
Fear of eating around other people
Skip meals before work or school
eat only a limited range of foods
Significant restriction may affect energy, concentration, medication use, and physical health.

Eating problems should not automatically be attributed to anxiety. Gastrointestinal illness, allergies, swallowing disorders, medication effects, pregnancy, eating disorders, and other conditions may need evaluation.
Inability to eat or drink safely, severe dehydration, fainting, confusion, or significant weakness requires urgent medical attention.
Anxiety may therefore affect daytime functioning even when anxious thoughts are strongest at night.
Anxiety can divide attention between the current task and possible threats.
They may appear distracted even though their mind is highly active.
For example, during a meeting, a person may be thinking about:
Whether they made a mistake earlier
Very little attention remains for the meeting itself.
Anxiety may interfere with working memory—the ability to hold and use information temporarily.
Forget why they entered a room
The problem may become worse when anxiety is combined with:
Persistent or rapidly worsening memory concerns should receive appropriate evaluation.
Anxiety can make decisions feel dangerous because every option appears to contain risk.
Functional problems may develop when decisions involve:
The person may not lack understanding. They may be waiting for certainty that cannot be achieved.
A task that normally takes 20 minutes may require several hours.
Internally, they may have spent the entire period trying to prevent mistakes or reduce uncertainty.
Treatment may help identify where time is being lost to anxiety-maintaining behaviors.
Fear of doing the task incorrectly
Physical symptoms in stores or public places
A person may clean one small area repeatedly while being unable to address essential tasks elsewhere.
Another may avoid beginning because the entire household feels overwhelming.
The goal is safe functioning rather than perfection.
Someone may be afraid to open financial mail because it could contain bad news.
Another person may check their bank account many times each day without developing a practical plan.
Mental health support may help address avoidance and decision-making, but qualified financial or legal guidance may also be necessary.
Anxiety may interfere with safe medication use.
Medication concerns should be discussed with the prescribing professional.

Anxiety does not make every side effect imaginary, and medication safety should be taken seriously. At the same time, repeated monitoring and fear may make it difficult to evaluate treatment accurately.
Patients should not start, stop, increase, decrease, or double medication without professional guidance.
Anxiety may prevent people from receiving appropriate healthcare.
Other people may seek healthcare repeatedly because they fear that ordinary physical sensations represent serious illness.
Both avoidance and repeated reassurance seeking can interfere with coordinated medical care.
Physical symptoms deserve appropriate evaluation. Mental health support may be helpful when fear continues controlling healthcare decisions despite reasonable assessment.
Driving restrictions may be appropriate when a person is affected by medication-related sedation, fainting, seizures, vision problems, or another medical condition.
These concerns require medical evaluation rather than being assumed to be anxiety.
Fear of buses, trains, airplanes, or other transportation may involve:
fear that help will be unavailable
The person may avoid travel or need a companion.
Severe restriction may occur with panic disorder, agoraphobia, social anxiety, specific phobias, trauma-related symptoms, or another condition.
Some people gradually limit how far they travel from home.
Avoidance may expand until the person:
remains close to one trusted person
The home may feel safe because escape and support are available.
However, increasing dependence on staying home can substantially limit daily functioning and quality of life.
Anxiety disorders can impair occupational functioning even when the employee remains present and appears productive.
Spending an hour reviewing a routine email
calling in sick because of anticipated panic
working late to recheck completed tasks
A person may meet expectations temporarily while becoming increasingly exhausted.
repeated requests to work from home
Attendance problems may be related to:
The pattern should be evaluated rather than dismissed as lack of motivation.
Anxiety may affect long-term career choices.
choose work only according to what feels least threatening
These choices may reduce anxiety temporarily while limiting development and financial opportunity.
Treatment may help the person distinguish genuine preferences from decisions controlled primarily by fear.
Anxiety can interfere with schoolwork and educational participation even when intellectual ability is unaffected.
A student may know the material but struggle to access it during an examination because attention is focused on fear and physical symptoms.
changing academic goals because of fear
High academic performance does not rule out impairment.
A student may maintain strong grades through:
The emotional and physical cost matters.
The person may want connection but fear:
Social anxiety may significantly affect work, relationships, and other daily activities when fear and avoidance become persistent.
The person may appear uninterested or unprepared when they are actually overwhelmed by fear.
Anxiety may affect intimate relationships through:
A partner may begin completing feared tasks or providing repeated reassurance.
This may help temporarily but can create strain and strengthen dependence.
Supportive treatment may focus on direct communication, boundaries, tolerating uncertainty, and gradually restoring independence.
Anxiety may interfere with parenting by causing:
Having anxiety does not mean someone is an uncaring or incapable parent.
Treatment may help the parent make decisions based on reasonable safety rather than anxiety alone.
Caregiver anxiety may require practical support, respite care, therapy, or medical and psychiatric evaluation.
Anxiety may make it difficult to:
Family members may misunderstand anxiety-driven avoidance as refusal or lack of care.
Clear communication and professional guidance may help the family respond without blame or overaccommodation.
The person may become increasingly isolated as fewer places feel manageable.
Reduced participation can remove sources of:
Treatment may aim not only to reduce symptoms but also to restore valued participation.
A person who fears body sensations may avoid exercise because it increases:
The person may interpret these normal changes as evidence of danger or an approaching panic attack.
A healthcare professional may need to assess whether exercise is medically safe before activity is increased.
Exercise can support wellbeing, but it should not be presented as a replacement for appropriate anxiety treatment.
Anxiety may affect functioning through repeated:
These behaviors may consume time, interrupt sleep, and reduce attention to work or relationships.
The question is not simply how much technology is used.
What purpose does the behavior serve?
What happens when checking is not possible?
Some people use alcohol, cannabis, sedatives, stimulants, or other substances to function despite anxiety.
This may create additional problems involving:
Mental health and substance-use concerns may need coordinated treatment.
Dangerous withdrawal, severe intoxication, or overdose requires emergency medical care.
A child may not describe anxiety directly.
Functional changes may be noticed first by:
Untreated childhood anxiety can interfere with academic progress, family relationships, and social development.
An evaluation should consider development, medical health, learning needs, bullying, trauma, family changes, and other possible conditions.
inability to plan for the future
A teenager may maintain grades while giving up friendships, sleep, and other activities.
Statements about self-harm, suicide, or having no reason to live require prompt attention.
Anxiety may affect older adults through:
New functional decline may also reflect:
Sudden confusion, fainting, weakness, or a rapid decline in ability should receive medical evaluation rather than being assumed to be anxiety.
Anxiety During Pregnancy and After Childbirth
A patient may experience repeated checking or intrusive, unwanted fears about harm.
Unwanted thoughts do not automatically mean the person intends to act. They should still be discussed honestly so the pattern and safety can be assessed.
Severe confusion, hallucinations, delusions, dangerous behavior, or intent to harm oneself or the baby requires emergency care.

What assistance do you now require?
Functional impairment helps the clinician understand severity and treatment needs, but it does not independently determine the diagnosis.
Treatment progress should not be measured only by asking whether anxiety feels lower.
A person may still feel some anxiety while becoming more able to complete meaningful activities.
The aim of treatment is not necessarily to eliminate every nervous feeling. It may be to help the person function safely and effectively without allowing anxiety to control important choices.
NIMH describes psychotherapy goals as relieving symptoms, maintaining or improving daily functioning, and supporting quality of life.
When anxiety has significantly limited activity, goals should be specific and manageable.
remain in a store for five minutes
eat one meal with another person
attend part of a social event
A goal should be challenging enough to support progress without being so overwhelming that it becomes unsafe or impossible to repeat.
Structured therapy can help plan gradual steps.
Exposure-based psychotherapy may help patients gradually learn to tolerate feared situations and sensations in a supportive setting rather than relying on avoidance.
The plan should be individualized according to:
Temporary practical support may help someone participate in treatment and rebuild independence.
Support should avoid permanently completing every feared activity when the person could gradually learn to participate.
The goal is usually to make recovery possible, not to create greater dependence.

When Functional Changes May Need Prompt Attention

Ordinary outpatient care may not be enough when someone:

Common Misconceptions About Anxiety and Functioning
“A Person Is Functioning Because They Still Work”
Employment does not reveal the time, distress, checking, substance use, avoidance, or exhaustion required to remain employed.
Some choices are genuine preferences. Others are controlled by fear and increasingly limit independence.
Difficulty beginning tasks, making decisions, concentrating, or leaving home may reflect anxiety rather than lack of care or effort.
“Helping With Every Task Is Always Supportive”
Temporary help may be valuable. Permanently completing every feared task can sometimes strengthen avoidance and dependence.
A student may maintain grades through severe overpreparation, poor sleep, panic, and social withdrawal.
“Physical Symptoms Do Not Count as Functional Impairment”
Nausea, dizziness, chest tightness, muscle tension, fatigue, and sleep disruption may directly affect daily activities.
“The Person Must Feel Calm Before Acting”
Many anxiety treatments help people complete meaningful activities while learning to tolerate manageable anxiety.
“One Productive Day Means the Problem Has Resolved”

children.text: Anxiety warning signs are changes that suggest fear, worry, physical tension, panic, avoidance, or related behaviors are becoming more frequent, intense, or disruptive.
They may appear before a person recognizes that their anxiety is worsening.
Feeling more irritable or on edge
Checking work, messages, health information, or safety concerns more often
Experiencing increasing muscle tension or digestive symptoms
Using more caffeine, alcohol, cannabis, or other substances
Feeling less able to manage ordinary responsibilities
Anxiety disorders involve more than occasional worry. Symptoms can persist, worsen over time, and interfere with work, school, relationships, and routine activities.

A warning sign does not automatically establish an anxiety disorder. Similar changes can occur with depression, trauma-related conditions, medication effects, substance use, sleep deprivation, bipolar disorder, medical illness, or major life stress.

The purpose of recognizing warning signs is not to label every uncomfortable feeling as a disorder. It is to notice meaningful changes early enough to review coping strategies, contact a healthcare professional, update a treatment plan, or seek urgent help when necessary.
For a broader explanation of anxiety symptoms, visit
Common Signs and Symptoms of Anxiety
What Is an Anxiety Warning Sign?
An anxiety warning sign is a change in thoughts, emotions, physical sensations, behavior, or daily functioning that may indicate anxiety is developing, returning, or becoming harder to manage.
The most useful warning signs are often personal.
For one person, worsening anxiety may begin with:
For another person, the first signs may be:
Someone who has experienced panic attacks may notice:
Recognizing an individual pattern can help the person respond before anxiety becomes severely disruptive.
Early warning signs may be subtle.
Feeling physically tense at the end of the day
Spending more time searching for information
Finding it harder to enjoy free time
These changes may not create major impairment at first.
However, they may indicate that anxiety is beginning to take more time, energy, and attention.
“Am I responding to a realistic problem, or am I spending increasing amounts of time trying to eliminate uncertainty?”
Worry That Is Becoming Harder to Control
Increasing worry is one of the most common warning signs.
The person may notice that worry:
Moves rapidly from one subject to another
Feels present even when nothing urgent is happening
“Even when I get an answer, I still do not feel settled.”
“I spend most of the day preparing for things that may never happen.”

Persistent and difficult-to-control worry, together with restlessness, fatigue, irritability, concentration problems, muscle tension, or sleep disturbance, may be part of generalized anxiety disorder.
Avoidance is an important warning sign because it can expand gradually.
A person may begin by avoiding:
That short-term relief can make avoidance more likely the next time, causing the person’s daily life to become increasingly restricted.
Making excuses to avoid feared situations
Depending on another person for routine activities
Choosing work or school activities only according to anxiety
Reassurance seeking may initially seem like ordinary support.
It becomes a warning sign when the person repeatedly asks:
“Do you think this symptom is serious?”
“Can you promise nothing bad will happen?”
The answer may provide relief briefly.
When anxiety returns, the person may:
Increasing reassurance seeking may indicate that the person is becoming less able to tolerate uncertainty or trust their own judgment.
It can also create strain in relationships.
Checking can become a warning sign when it increases in frequency, duration, or importance.
Reasonable checking supports safety and accuracy.
Continue after the person knows the task is complete
Increase doubt instead of resolving it
Cause conflict with family or coworkers
Repeated checking may also occur with obsessive-compulsive disorder, which is diagnostically separate from anxiety disorders and may require specialized evaluation.
Sleep changes are often an early sign that anxiety is worsening.
Checking messages or locks at night
Depending increasingly on alcohol, cannabis, or sleep products
Consistently poor sleep can occur with anxiety and other mental health conditions.

A sudden reduced need for sleep combined with unusually high energy, rapid speech, increased confidence, impulsivity, or risk-taking should be reported promptly because it may indicate mania, hypomania, medication activation, or another condition rather than anxiety alone.
Anxiety may appear as irritability rather than visible fear.
Feeling angry when reassurance is unavailable
Becoming increasingly sensitive to noise or crowds
Having more conflict at home or work
Irritability may develop because the person is:
SAMHSA identifies feeling edgy, angry, worried, scared, or increasingly disconnected from others as possible warning signs of emotional distress.
Irritability can also occur with depression, trauma, ADHD, bipolar disorder, substance use, medication effects, and medical conditions.
Worsening anxiety may show up through the body.
A person may notice that physical symptoms are occurring:
Before activities that were previously manageable
Anxiety can produce genuine physical symptoms, but new, severe, or changing symptoms should not automatically be attributed to anxiety.
A person may begin paying close attention to:
They may interpret ordinary sensations as signs of:
Physical symptoms deserve appropriate medical assessment. Mental health support may also be useful when fear continues despite reasonable evaluation and begins controlling daily life.
Increasing panic attacks are a clear warning sign that anxiety care may need review.
Signs that panic is becoming more disruptive include:
Using alcohol or medication outside instructions to prevent panic
Panic attacks can occur with panic disorder and several other psychiatric or medical conditions.
A new or unfamiliar episode may require medical evaluation, particularly when symptoms include severe chest pain, fainting, neurological changes, or major breathing difficulty.
A person may begin limiting how far they travel from home.
Working only from home because of fear
Increasing restriction may occur with panic disorder, agoraphobia, social anxiety, trauma-related symptoms, or another condition.
Taking longer to complete ordinary tasks
Working late because nothing feels complete
Calling in sick because of anticipated panic
The person may still appear productive.
The warning sign may be the amount of distress, time, and exhaustion required to maintain performance.
Anxiety disorders may interfere with job performance and other routine responsibilities.
Anxiety warning signs in school or college may include:
Sleeping poorly before ordinary school days
Using substances to manage academic anxiety
A student may maintain good grades while experiencing severe anxiety, perfectionism, sleep loss, and social withdrawal.
Academic performance alone does not show the full level of impairment.
Decision-making problems may become a warning sign when the person:
Feels unable to act without certainty
Increasing indecision can affect healthcare, employment, relationships, finances, and daily responsibilities.
Anxiety may be worsening when relationships become increasingly organized around fear.
Checking another person’s messages or location
Depending on one person for ordinary tasks
A partner or family member may begin adjusting their own life to prevent the person from becoming anxious.
Compassionate support can be helpful, but repeated accommodation may sometimes strengthen avoidance and dependence.
Social withdrawal may occur because the person:
Does not want others to notice symptoms
Pulling away from people and usual activities can be an early warning sign of emotional or mental health difficulty.
Social withdrawal may also indicate depression, trauma, substance use, psychosis, or another concern.
Anxiety may affect eating through nausea, stomach tension, fear of choking, fear of vomiting, social anxiety, or fear of allergic reactions.
Eating only when another person is present
Avoiding food before work, school, or travel
Feeling unable to eat because of worry
Eating or sleeping much more or much less than usual may be a warning sign of broader emotional distress.
Significant weight loss, dehydration, fainting, swallowing difficulty, or inability to eat safely requires medical evaluation.
A person may increase caffeine because anxiety-related sleep loss is causing fatigue.
The person may then interpret these symptoms as evidence that anxiety is worsening or that something medically dangerous is happening.

Reducing excessive caffeine may support anxiety care, but severe or persistent symptoms still require appropriate evaluation. NIMH notes that reducing caffeine and obtaining adequate sleep may help reduce anxiety symptoms when used alongside standard treatment.
A person may use alcohol, cannabis, sedatives, stimulants, or other substances to:
Needing more to achieve the same effect
Being unable to attend events without using
SAMHSA identifies increased smoking, drinking, drug use, or misuse of prescription medication as a warning sign of emotional distress.
Anxiety and substance-use concerns may need coordinated treatment.
Dangerous withdrawal, overdose, or severe intoxication requires emergency medical care.
This may happen because the person is:
A major decline in self-care deserves prompt clinical attention.
An inability to complete daily tasks, care for children, or attend work or school can be an important warning sign of a mental health problem.
A person may become increasingly dependent on another person to:
The warning sign is a continuing loss of independence, especially when the person becomes unable to perform activities they previously managed.
Treatment may help the person rebuild independence gradually rather than removing all support at once.
Children may not describe anxiety directly.
Frequent visits to the school nurse
Seek evaluation when these changes persist, worsen, interfere with development, or significantly affect school and family life.
Anxiety warning signs in teenagers may include:
A teenager may maintain grades while experiencing severe internal distress.
Comments about death, self-harm, or having no reason to live should never be dismissed as attention-seeking.
Older adults may show worsening anxiety through:
New anxiety in an older adult may also reflect:
Sudden confusion, weakness, fainting, falls, or rapid functional decline requires medical evaluation and should not automatically be attributed to anxiety.
Warning Signs During Pregnancy or After Childbirth
Anxiety may worsen during pregnancy or after delivery.
Avoiding being alone with the baby
Feeling unable to care for the baby
Unwanted intrusive thoughts do not automatically mean that the person intends to act.
They should still be discussed honestly so the clinician can assess the pattern, distress, and safety.
Severe confusion, hallucinations, delusions, dangerous behavior, or intent to harm oneself or the baby requires emergency care.
Warning Signs That the Current Treatment May Need Review
A person already receiving anxiety treatment may need a follow-up when:
Side effects are interfering with treatment
The person wants to stop medication
Therapy exercises are no longer being used
Work or school functioning is declining
The care plan no longer fits current circumstances
A treatment review may lead to:
The patient should not stop, restart, increase, decrease, or double medication without guidance from the prescribing professional.
Warning Signs of Possible Medication Effects
Contact the prescribing professional when anxiety begins or becomes significantly worse after:
Do not make independent medication changes unless emergency medical professionals instruct otherwise.
Warning Signs of Depression Alongside Anxiety
The combination of anxiety and depression can significantly increase distress, impairment, and safety concerns.
Statements such as the following require prompt attention:
“I do not want to wake up.”
Warning Signs of Possible Mania or Hypomania
Symptoms that appear to be anxiety may sometimes reflect mania, hypomania, medication activation, stimulant effects, or another condition.
Sleeping very little without feeling tired
With anxiety-related insomnia, the person usually wants to sleep and feels tired.
With mania or hypomania, the person may have a reduced need for sleep while remaining unusually energetic.
Warning Signs of Psychosis or Severe Confusion
Severe anxiety alone does not usually explain persistent hallucinations, fixed false beliefs, or major confusion.
Urgent assessment is needed when a person:
Hears voices others do not hear
Sees things others do not see
Believes others are controlling or targeting them without clear evidence
Behaves in a dangerous or highly disorganized way
SAMHSA includes hearing voices, believing things that are not true, severe confusion, and inability to complete daily tasks among warning signs that mental health support may be needed.
Severe psychosis, dangerous behavior, or inability to remain safe requires emergency care.
Anxiety disorders can occur alongside suicidal thoughts or behavior, particularly when severe anxiety is combined with depression, substance use, trauma, pain, major losses, or social isolation.
Saying there is no reason to live
A sudden unexplained calm after severe distress
Thoughts of hurting oneself or another person require immediate attention.
Do not promise secrecy when someone is in immediate danger.
Routine, Prompt, and Emergency Warning Signs
It can be helpful to divide warning signs into levels.
Contact the provider if symptoms continue
Signs to Contact a Professional Promptly
NIMH recommends speaking with a healthcare professional when symptoms worsen or self-care efforts are not helping.
Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room when someone:
Has a suicide plan and intends to act
Has immediate access to lethal means
When Physical Symptoms May Be a Medical Emergency
Anxiety and panic can cause chest tightness, rapid heartbeat, shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, and dizziness.
Similar symptoms can occur during serious medical emergencies.
Chest pain with sweating, nausea, dizziness, or shortness of breath
MedlinePlus advises immediate medical care for persistent or crushing chest pain and chest pain accompanied by symptoms such as nausea, sweating, dizziness, or shortness of breath.
Do not delay emergency assessment because similar symptoms occurred during a previous panic attack.
Creating a Personal Anxiety Warning-Sign List
A personal warning-sign list can help the patient identify changes earlier.
The list should also identify what action to take when each sign appears.
What to Do When Warning Signs Appear
Avoid increasing alcohol or other substances
Contact the therapist or psychiatric provider
The response should match the severity of the warning signs.
A mild increase in worry may call for monitoring and routine support.
Suicidal intent, severe psychosis, overdose, or inability to remain safe requires emergency care.
How Family and Friends Can Respond
A supportive person may notice warning signs before the individual recognizes them.
“You are sleeping only a few hours.”
“You have called out of work several times.”
“You are checking your blood pressure throughout the day.”
“You are drinking more to calm yourself.”
“You have said that you cannot keep going.”
Calling emergency services during immediate danger
Telling the person to calm down

SAMHSA recommends recognizing significant changes and helping the person connect with appropriate professional support when anxiety, worry, sleep problems, or irritability become intense, persistent, or disruptive.
How Anxiety Warning Signs Are Evaluated
How sleep and eating are affected
Whether work or school is affected
The clinician may consider whether symptoms are related to:
Before an appointment, consider writing down:
“I have had four panic attacks this month, stopped driving on highways, sleep about four hours, and call my sister several times each day for reassurance.”
Can Warning Signs Appear After Improvement?
Anxiety symptoms may improve and later return during:
Recognizing these signs early may help the person update treatment before severe impairment returns.
Common Misconceptions About Anxiety Warning Signs
“Warning Signs Only Matter During a Panic Attack”
Worsening anxiety may appear through sleep changes, avoidance, irritability, checking, reassurance seeking, or declining functioning without panic attacks.
“The Person Is Fine Because They Still Work”
Someone may remain employed while experiencing severe worry, overpreparation, poor sleep, physical symptoms, and exhaustion.
Avoidance may reduce fear briefly while allowing anxiety and dependence to grow.
Reassurance can be compassionate, but repeated reassurance that provides only temporary relief may maintain the anxiety cycle.
Anxiety can produce real physical symptoms. Concerning symptoms still require appropriate medical evaluation.
“Sudden High Energy Means the Anxiety Is Improving”
High energy with reduced need for sleep, rapid speech, impulsivity, or unusual confidence may suggest mania, hypomania, medication activation, or substance effects.
Alcohol or substances may be used to manage anxiety and can worsen symptoms, create dependence, and affect safety.
“Suicidal Thoughts Are Not Part of Anxiety”
Severe anxiety may occur with depression, substance use, trauma, and suicidal thinking. Every suicide warning sign should be taken seriously.
Warning signs show that further attention may be needed. Diagnosis requires evaluation of the full pattern and other possible causes.
Seek professional help when anxiety warning signs:
A person does not need to wait until all areas of life are affected.
When to Seek Help for Anxiety
Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room when someone:
May harm themselves or another person
Has a suicide plan and intends to act
Has immediate access to lethal means
Has severe or unfamiliar chest pain
Has sudden weakness or difficulty speaking
Tinka Health Services is not an emergency service.
Do not wait for a scheduled appointment, website response, voicemail, email, or patient portal message during an immediate emergency.

sections.title: Diagnosis

children.text: Anxiety is evaluated through a clinical assessment of a person’s symptoms, fears, physical sensations, behavior, medical history, substance use, daily functioning, and current safety.
There is no single blood test, brain scan, online quiz, or physical symptom that can independently diagnose an anxiety disorder.
What are you worried or afraid about?
How long have the symptoms been present?
Are the worries difficult to control?
Is work, school, parenting, or self-care affected?
Are medications, caffeine, alcohol, or other substances involved?
Are depression, trauma, obsessive thoughts, or mood changes also present?
Have thoughts of self-harm or suicide occurred?

The evaluation may also include a physical-health review, screening questionnaires, previous treatment records, observations from a trusted person when appropriate, and medical testing when another condition may be contributing.
Anxiety disorders are generally diagnosed when fear or worry is persistent, disproportionate to the situation, difficult to manage, and interfering with daily functioning.

A complete evaluation does more than confirm whether anxiety exists. It helps identify the specific pattern, consider alternative explanations, assess severity and safety, and develop an individualized treatment plan.
What Happens During an Anxiety Evaluation?
An anxiety evaluation usually begins with a conversation about what the patient has been experiencing.
The exact questions depend on the patient’s age, symptoms, history, and reason for seeking care.
Someone reporting constant worry may be asked different questions from someone reporting panic attacks, fear of social judgment, avoidance of driving, or anxiety about a specific medical procedure.
The clinician may also ask questions that do not appear directly related to anxiety. These questions help identify other conditions that can produce similar symptoms or occur at the same time.
What Is the Main Goal of the Evaluation?
The purpose of an anxiety evaluation is to understand:
Whether another condition may be involved
What level of care is appropriate
Which treatment options may fit the patient
The goal is not to judge whether the person should be able to control the anxiety.
It is also not to force every patient into one diagnosis or treatment approach.
A careful evaluation may result in:
Recognition of more than one condition
A recommendation for further medical assessment
A treatment plan without an immediate final diagnosis
Referral to another professional or level of care
Some diagnostic questions can be answered during the first appointment. Others require follow-up, previous records, medical testing, or observation over time.
How Does a Clinician Begin the Conversation?
The clinician may begin with open questions such as:
What are you avoiding because of anxiety?
How is this affecting your daily life?
What do you hope to receive help with?
The patient does not need to use perfect clinical language.
Statements such as the following can provide useful starting information:
“I worry for several hours almost every day.”
“I am having sudden episodes where my heart races and I feel like I will die.”
“I cannot speak during meetings even when I know what I want to say.”
“I keep checking my work because I am afraid of making a mistake.”
“I cannot sleep because my mind will not stop.”
“I need reassurance from my family throughout the day.”
Specific examples often help the clinician understand the pattern more clearly than a general statement such as “I am stressed.”
The clinician may ask about emotional symptoms such as:
The clinician looks at the overall combination rather than using one symptom as proof of a diagnosis.
For a detailed symptom guide, visit
Common Signs and Symptoms of Anxiety
The timing of symptoms can provide important diagnostic information.
Did it begin gradually or suddenly?
Did it begin during childhood, adolescence, or adulthood?
Did symptoms begin after an illness?
Did symptoms begin after medication or substance use?
Have there been previous periods of similar anxiety?
A sudden onset may raise questions about:
An anxiety disorder can also begin without one identifiable event.
The absence of a clear cause does not make the symptoms less real.
Duration helps distinguish a temporary stress response from a persistent anxiety pattern.
How many days each week are affected?
How long does the anxiety last?
How often do panic attacks occur?
How long has avoidance been present?
Different anxiety disorders have different diagnostic patterns and duration requirements.

For example, generalized anxiety disorder commonly involves excessive worry across several areas of life over an extended period, while panic disorder involves recurring unexpected panic attacks followed by ongoing concern or behavioral changes.
The clinician interprets duration together with severity, impairment, age, development, and context.
Different anxiety disorders are often distinguished partly by what triggers the fear.
The clinician may ask whether anxiety centers on:
The same physical symptom may appear in several conditions.
For example, a rapid heartbeat may occur with:
The meaning, trigger, timing, and associated behavior help clarify the pattern.
When generalized anxiety disorder is being considered, the clinician may ask whether the patient:
Worries excessively about several areas of life
Finds the worry difficult to control
Generalized anxiety disorder is characterized by excessive worry that is difficult to control and may cause meaningful impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of life.
The clinician also considers whether the worry is better explained by another condition, substance, medication, or realistic ongoing crisis.
Evaluating Panic Attacks and Panic Disorder
The clinician may ask whether the patient experiences sudden periods of intense fear or discomfort involving:
Are you afraid of having another attack?
Have you changed your behavior because of the attacks?
A panic attack alone does not confirm panic disorder.
Panic attacks can occur with other anxiety disorders, trauma-related conditions, depression, substance use, medication effects, and medical problems.

Medical assessment may be needed because panic symptoms can resemble heart, breathing, neurological, or metabolic conditions. MedlinePlus notes that evaluation of recurring panic symptoms may include determining whether they are caused by panic disorder or a physical condition.
When social anxiety is being considered, the clinician may ask whether the patient fears:
Does the fear occur before, during, or after the event?
Are work, school, relationships, or healthcare affected?
Do you use alcohol or another substance to participate socially?
Is the fear stronger than ordinary shyness?
Social anxiety may include rapid heartbeat, sweating, trembling, nausea, mental blankness, difficulty making eye contact, and avoidance of social situations despite wanting connection.
A specific phobia involves intense fear of a particular object or situation.
The clinician may ask about fear of:
Does fear begin immediately when you encounter the trigger?
Do you endure it with severe distress?
How does the fear affect healthcare, travel, work, or relationships?
Is the fear proportionate to the actual danger?
The clinician may also consider trauma, panic disorder, medical concerns, sensory issues, and obsessive-compulsive symptoms.
When agoraphobia is being considered, the clinician may ask about fear involving:
They will become unable to function
The clinician may ask whether the patient:
The assessment focuses on both the feared situation and the functional limitations that have developed.
Avoidance is a major part of many anxiety evaluations.
What activities have you stopped doing?
Do you need another person with you?
Have you changed work, school, or travel plans?
Is your daily life becoming smaller?
The person may initially describe avoidance as preference or convenience.
The clinician may explore whether the choice is based primarily on fear and whether it is reducing independence or quality of life.
The clinician may ask whether the patient repeatedly:
Asks others whether everything is okay
Monitors heart rate or blood pressure
These behaviors may be attempts to reduce uncertainty.
How much time do they take?
What happens if checking is prevented?
Repeated checking and reassurance can occur with anxiety disorders, illness anxiety, or obsessive-compulsive disorder.
The specific thoughts and purpose of the behavior help with diagnostic clarification.
A diagnosis should not be based only on the presence of symptoms.
The clinician also evaluates how anxiety affects functioning.
Are you bathing and grooming regularly?
Are you eating and drinking adequately?
How much time is spent checking work?
Can you drive or use transportation?
Functional impairment helps the clinician understand severity and treatment needs.
How Anxiety Can Affect Daily Functioning
Sleep is an important part of an anxiety evaluation.
Poor sleep may result from anxiety, but the clinician may also consider:
The distinction between insomnia and reduced need for sleep is especially important.
A person with anxiety-related insomnia usually wants to sleep and feels tired.
A person experiencing mania or hypomania may sleep very little while remaining unusually energetic, active, confident, or impulsive.
Anxiety-like symptoms can be caused or worsened by physical-health conditions.

MedlinePlus explains that anxiety evaluation may involve a symptom and medical-history review, physical examination, and laboratory testing to check whether another health condition is causing the symptoms.
A psychiatric provider may recommend coordination with primary care or another specialist when appropriate.
The clinician may ask for a complete list of:
Did anxiety begin after a medication started?
Did symptoms change after a dose adjustment?
Are several stimulating products being combined?
Patients should not stop prescribed medication independently because they suspect it is contributing.
Medication concerns should be reviewed with the prescribing professional.
Caffeine and nicotine may contribute to:
The amount, frequency, timing, and relationship to symptoms are important.
A person may increase caffeine to compensate for anxiety-related sleep loss, creating a cycle of greater physical arousal and poorer sleep.
Anxiety evaluation should include an honest discussion of:
Does it help you sleep or socialize?
Substance intoxication and withdrawal can cause or worsen:
Anxiety and substance-use concerns may need coordinated treatment.
Dangerous withdrawal, overdose, or severe intoxication requires medical care.
Previous response can guide the current plan.
Did treatment end because of cost or access?
Were appointments missed because of anxiety?
The goal is not to judge past treatment decisions.
It is to learn from them.
The clinician may ask whether close relatives have experienced:
Family history does not determine the diagnosis.
It may provide useful context because genetic and environmental factors can influence mental health risk.
The clinician may also ask how family members respond to anxiety, including whether they provide support, reassurance, or assistance with avoided activities.
Anxiety and depression commonly occur together.
Someone may experience both fear about the future and hopelessness that the future will improve.
The presence of depression may affect:
Anxiety, agitation, insomnia, and racing thoughts can also occur during mania or hypomania.
The clinician may ask whether the patient has ever experienced a period involving:
Much less sleep without feeling tired
A person may describe a hypomanic period as a time when they were unusually productive or social.
Screening is important because treatment recommendations may differ when bipolar disorder is present.
The clinician may ask about trauma when the patient reports:
The patient should not be forced to provide detailed trauma information before they are ready.
A trauma-informed evaluation may focus initially on:
Post-traumatic stress disorder is classified separately from anxiety disorders, although fear and anxiety can be prominent.
The clinician may ask whether the patient experiences:
Obsessive-compulsive disorder is diagnostically separate from anxiety disorders.
The distinction matters because specialized psychotherapy may be recommended.
What thought comes before the behavior?
What does the person fear will happen?
How much time does it consume?
What happens if it is resisted?
Anxiety and ADHD can both involve:
Were attention problems present in childhood?
Do they occur even when the person is not anxious?
Is attention mainly disrupted by worry?
Are there long-standing difficulties with organization and impulse control?
A careful developmental history helps prevent every concentration problem from being attributed to anxiety.
Severe anxiety does not usually explain persistent hallucinations, fixed false beliefs, or major disorganization.
Seeing things others do not see
Psychotic symptoms may require urgent or specialized assessment.
The clinician may need to consider:
An anxiety evaluation should include direct questions about safety.
Access to firearms or excess medication
These questions do not place the idea of suicide in someone’s mind.
They help determine the appropriate level of care.
Anxiety disorders may coexist with depression, substance use, trauma, and suicidal thoughts. A patient should disclose these thoughts honestly, even if there is no immediate plan.
Reporting suicidal thoughts does not automatically result in hospitalization. The clinician considers:
Ability to follow a safe outpatient plan
Emergency care may be needed when the person cannot remain safe.
Yes. A clinician may use a standardized questionnaire to support the evaluation.
A questionnaire may ask how often the patient has recently experienced:
fear that something bad will happen
APA assessment measures are designed to support initial clinical interviews and help monitor patient-reported symptoms over time.
A screening result is not the same as a diagnosis.
A low score does not rule out a situation-specific anxiety disorder, severe avoidance, or symptoms the questionnaire did not capture.
The GAD-7 is a brief questionnaire commonly used to screen for generalized anxiety symptoms and estimate their severity.
It asks about experiences such as:
Fear that something bad will happen
The score may help organize the clinical discussion and track change.
SAMHSA identifies the GAD-7 as a questionnaire used to screen for generalized anxiety symptoms and assess recent symptom severity.
During the appointment, the clinician may observe:
For example, the clinician may notice:
These observations are considered together with the patient’s report.
A calm appearance does not rule out significant anxiety. Some patients appear composed while experiencing severe internal distress.
Not everyone undergoing an anxiety evaluation needs laboratory testing.
Testing may be recommended when symptoms, history, age, medication, or physical-health concerns suggest another possible cause.
The specific tests depend on the clinical situation.

There is no laboratory test that confirms generalized anxiety disorder. Diagnosis is based on the clinical history, while physical examination or testing may help rule out conditions with similar symptoms.
When Heart or Breathing Symptoms Need Medical Evaluation
Similar symptoms can occur with serious physical conditions.
A clinician may recommend medical evaluation when symptoms are:
Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room for severe or unfamiliar chest pain, major breathing difficulty, fainting, sudden weakness, difficulty speaking, or another possible medical emergency.
Do not assume a serious physical symptom is only anxiety because the person has a history of panic attacks.
Children may not describe anxiety using adult language.
The evaluation may include information from:
Symptoms should be considered in relation to age and development.
The child may be given an opportunity to speak privately when developmentally and clinically appropriate.
Parents or guardians may notice changes the teenager does not report.
The teenager’s private perspective is also important.
A young person may maintain high grades while experiencing severe anxiety, sleep loss, social withdrawal, or substance use.
Evaluation in older adults may include careful review of:
Anxiety may be expressed mainly through physical symptoms or repeated medical concerns.
New anxiety, confusion, weakness, or rapid functional change may require medical assessment.
The clinician should avoid assuming that every new symptom is psychological or an unavoidable part of aging.
Evaluation During Pregnancy or After Childbirth
Anxiety evaluation during pregnancy or postpartum may include:
ability to care for the baby
Unwanted intrusive thoughts do not automatically mean the person intends to act.
Severe confusion, hallucinations, delusions, dangerous behavior, or intent to harm oneself or the baby requires emergency care.
Can Anxiety Be Evaluated Through Telehealth?
Many parts of an anxiety evaluation can be completed through secure video when telehealth is clinically appropriate.
During a telehealth evaluation, the provider may confirm:
Telehealth does not replace physical examination, laboratory testing, or emergency assessment when those services are needed.
Eligible patients physically located in Maryland, Washington, DC, or Virginia may be able to receive telehealth care through Tinka Health Services when virtual treatment is clinically appropriate.

The clinician may also speak privately with the patient for part of the appointment.
Family involvement should support rather than silence or control the patient.
What If the Patient Does Not Remember Every Detail?
A patient is not expected to remember every date, medication, or symptom perfectly.
The patient should not delay care because the information is incomplete.
The provider can identify which missing details are most important.
Will the Patient Receive a Diagnosis During the First Visit?
A diagnosis may be made during the first visit when the symptom pattern is clear and sufficient information is available.
In other cases, the clinician may need:
The clinician may use a provisional diagnosis while gathering additional information.
A provisional diagnosis does not mean the symptoms are unimportant or that care cannot begin.
Safety, sleep, functioning, substance use, and immediate treatment needs can still be addressed.
After the evaluation, the provider may discuss:
What the provider thinks may be happening
What the recommended next step is
What to do if symptoms worsen
Questions to Ask During an Anxiety Evaluation
What anxiety disorder are you considering?
Could a medical condition be contributing?
Do I need physical examination or laboratory testing?
Are my medications or supplements affecting symptoms?
Could caffeine or substance use be involved?
Are panic attacks part of the diagnosis?
Have depression and bipolar disorder been considered?
What screening tool did you use?
Do you recommend therapy, medication, or both?
When should I go to the emergency room?
A questionnaire may identify symptoms and support further evaluation. It cannot independently establish the full diagnosis.
“A Blood Test Confirms an Anxiety Disorder”
There is no routine blood test that confirms an anxiety disorder. Tests may be used to look for other medical explanations.
“Physical Symptoms Mean the Problem Cannot Be Anxiety”
Anxiety can produce real physical symptoms. Medical conditions still need to be considered when appropriate.
“Normal Medical Tests Mean the Symptoms Are Imaginary”
Normal results do not mean the distress is invented. They may help narrow the possible causes.
A complete assessment may review panic, avoidance, physical symptoms, sleep, functioning, medication, substances, trauma, depression, bipolar symptoms, and safety.
Some patients hide anxiety effectively or remain calm during a structured appointment despite severe symptoms elsewhere.
“A Diagnosis Must Be Made in One Appointment”
Some cases require additional records, testing, follow-up, or observation.
An evaluation does not guarantee a prescription. Treatment depends on the clinical findings, preferences, risks, and alternatives.
The clinician evaluates plan, intent, access to means, history, support, and ability to remain safe. Hospital care may be needed when outpatient treatment is not sufficient for safety.

children.text: Preparing for an anxiety evaluation can help you describe your symptoms clearly, remember important details, ask useful questions, and understand the next steps in your care.
You do not need to arrive with a diagnosis or explain everything perfectly.
Before the appointment, it may help to gather:
A list of your main anxiety symptoms
Examples of how anxiety affects daily life
Alcohol, caffeine, nicotine, and substance use
Information about thoughts of self-harm or suicide

An anxiety evaluation is usually based on a detailed conversation about symptoms, physical sensations, behavior, medical history, daily functioning, treatment history, and safety. A clinician may also recommend a physical examination or laboratory testing when another health condition could be contributing.
Preparation can make the conversation easier, but incomplete notes should never prevent you from attending.
An anxiety evaluation is a clinical assessment used to understand whether fear, worry, panic, physical symptoms, avoidance, or related behaviors may be caused by:
What you fear or worry about
How difficult the worry is to control
Whether you repeatedly check or seek reassurance
How symptoms affect work, school, relationships, and self-care
The purpose is not simply to confirm that you feel anxious. It is to understand the full pattern and determine what type of support may be appropriate.
For more information about the assessment process, visit
Do You Need to Prepare for an Anxiety Evaluation?
You can attend an anxiety evaluation without preparing anything in advance.
However, anxiety itself may make it difficult to:
A short written summary can reduce the pressure to remember everything during the conversation.
NIMH recommends thinking about questions and concerns before discussing mental health with a healthcare professional because appointment time may be limited.
Preparation should support the appointment rather than become another source of perfectionism.
A one-page note with the most important information is often more useful than trying to create a complete life history.
Start With the Main Reason You Are Seeking Help
Consider writing one or two sentences that explain why you scheduled the appointment.
“I worry for several hours most days and cannot control it.”
“I have started having panic attacks and avoiding driving.”
“I am afraid of being judged and have stopped attending meetings.”
“Physical symptoms are making it difficult for me to leave home.”
“I cannot sleep because my mind does not stop.”
“My anxiety is interfering with school and relationships.”
“I need help understanding whether my symptoms are anxiety or something else.”
This summary gives the clinician a starting point.
You do not need to know the name of the disorder.
Make a List of Your Anxiety Symptoms
Write down the symptoms you have noticed.
Fear that something bad will happen
Using alcohol or substances to cope
You do not need to have every symptom associated with anxiety.
For a fuller symptom guide, visit
Common Signs and Symptoms of Anxiety
Your approximate age when symptoms started
Whether the symptoms began gradually or suddenly
Whether they followed a stressful event
Whether they began after an illness
Whether they began after starting or stopping a medication
Exact dates are not always necessary.
Statements such as these may be enough:
“The panic attacks began about three months ago.”
“I have worried this way since childhood.”
“Symptoms became worse after I changed jobs.”
“The physical symptoms started after a medication dose changed.”
“I felt better for several years, but the anxiety returned recently.”
Timing can help the clinician distinguish a long-term anxiety pattern from a medication effect, medical condition, withdrawal state, or temporary response to stress.
The clinician may ask about frequency.
During particular times of the month
After caffeine, alcohol, or another substance
“Monday: worried for about four hours, skipped lunch, checked my work repeatedly, slept five hours.”
“Wednesday: panic symptoms while driving, pulled over, called my sister, avoided driving for the rest of the day.”
When panic attacks occur, write down:
Whether there was an obvious trigger
What you did to escape or feel safe
Whether you now avoid that situation
A panic attack does not automatically establish panic disorder. The clinician considers whether attacks recur, whether they are unexpected, and whether fear or avoidance continues afterward.
Avoidance is an important part of an anxiety evaluation.
Arrange your life around preventing anxiety
Avoidance may provide temporary relief while increasing functional limitations over time.
Tell the clinician if you repeatedly:
Ask whether someone is angry with you
Monitor your heart rate or blood pressure
Ask several people the same question
What happens if you cannot check
These patterns can occur with anxiety disorders, illness anxiety, or obsessive-compulsive symptoms.
Explain How Anxiety Affects Daily Functioning
Specific examples can help the clinician understand severity.
“I have missed work twice this month, stopped driving on highways, and call my partner several times a day for reassurance.”
How Anxiety Can Affect Daily Functioning
Bring a list of all medications and products you use.
Medication bottles, pharmacy records, or photographs of labels may be helpful.
The clinician may need to determine whether symptoms changed after:
Do not stop prescribed medication abruptly before the appointment unless a qualified professional has instructed you to do so.
If you have previously taken medication for anxiety, depression, sleep, ADHD, or another mental health concern, record:
Whether it caused agitation or unusual energy
Do not worry if you cannot remember every detail.
“I took an antidepressant several years ago but do not remember the name.”
“A medication helped panic but made me too sleepy.”
“I stopped because I lost insurance coverage.”
Previous response can help guide future recommendations.
Tell the clinician about current and previous medical conditions, including:
Anxiety-like symptoms can sometimes be related to physical-health conditions. A clinician may recommend examination or testing when appropriate.
List Allergies and Serious Medication Reactions
Distinguish between an allergy and a side effect when possible.
“This medication caused nausea” may describe a side effect.
“This medication caused facial swelling and breathing difficulty” may describe a serious allergic reaction.
The clinician can help clarify how the reaction should be documented.
Caffeine and nicotine may affect anxiety, sleep, heart rate, and physical tension.
Whether you use caffeine because you are sleeping poorly
Do not minimize caffeine or nicotine because they are legal or commonly used. Accurate information helps the clinician understand your symptom pattern.
Be Honest About Alcohol and Substance Use
Whether you use it to sleep or socialize
Whether substances are combined with medication
Substances may cause, worsen, or temporarily mask anxiety symptoms.
This information is clinically important and should not be treated as a moral judgment.
SAMHSA encourages openness about mental health, alcohol, and drug concerns when arranging or attending care.
Dangerous withdrawal, overdose, or severe intoxication requires urgent medical care and should not wait for a routine anxiety evaluation.
Consider whether you have previously experienced:
Past records may be useful, but you do not need to delay the appointment while trying to obtain every document.
The clinician may ask whether close relatives have experienced:
You may not know every diagnosis.
Statements such as these are still useful:
“My brother was treated for bipolar disorder.”
“There is a history of suicide attempts in my family.”
Family history can provide context, but it does not determine your diagnosis.
Tell the clinician if you are sleeping much less than usual.
Feel tired and want to sleep
Feel unusually energetic despite very little sleep
Reduced need for sleep with unusual energy may require evaluation for mania, hypomania, medication activation, or substance effects rather than anxiety alone.
Anxiety and depression can occur together.
Do not leave these symptoms out because the appointment is “for anxiety.”
They may affect diagnosis, treatment, follow-up, and safety planning.
Prepare to Discuss Trauma Without Forcing Details
The clinician may ask whether difficult or traumatic experiences contribute to:
You do not need to provide every detail of a traumatic event during the first appointment.
“I have a trauma history that affects my sleep.”
“Certain situations remind me of something that happened.”
“I am not ready to discuss the details today.”
“I would like help with the symptoms first.”
A trauma-informed evaluation should respect your pace while still assessing current symptoms and safety.
Prepare to Discuss Obsessive Thoughts and Repetitive Behaviors
Tell the clinician if you experience:
These symptoms may be related to obsessive-compulsive disorder rather than, or in addition to, an anxiety disorder.
What thought comes before the behavior?
What do you fear will happen?
How much time does it take?
What happens if you do not perform the behavior?
Honest description helps guide appropriate treatment.
Prepare to Discuss Possible Mania or Hypomania
The clinician may ask whether you have experienced periods involving:
Very little sleep without feeling tired
These questions help distinguish anxiety from bipolar-spectrum symptoms, stimulant effects, medication activation, or another condition.
A past period may have felt productive or enjoyable rather than distressing.
Include it even if you did not consider it a problem at the time.
Prepare to Discuss Self-Harm and Suicide Honestly
An anxiety evaluation may include direct questions about:
Access to firearms or excess medication
Be honest even if the thoughts feel embarrassing or frightening.

Reporting thoughts of death or suicide does not automatically mean you will be hospitalized. The clinician considers the nature of the thoughts, plan, intent, access to means, history, support, judgment, and ability to remain safe.
However, do not wait for a scheduled evaluation if you intend to act, have attempted suicide, have taken an overdose, or cannot remain safe.
Consider what you most want to change.
Goals help the clinician understand what recovery would look like for you.
Treatment does not always aim to remove every feeling of nervousness. It may help you function more freely and respond differently to fear and uncertainty.
What type of anxiety are you considering?
Could a medical condition be contributing?
Do I need laboratory testing or a physical examination?
Could medication or caffeine be affecting me?
Are my panic attacks part of panic disorder?
Could trauma or obsessive-compulsive symptoms be involved?
Have depression and bipolar disorder been considered?
Do you recommend therapy, medication, or both?
What type of therapy may help?
What should I do if symptoms worsen?
Which symptoms require urgent or emergency care?
Can treatment be provided through telehealth?
What costs or insurance questions should I clarify?
Do not delay care if you cannot obtain them.
You may be asked to sign an authorization before one healthcare professional can communicate with another.
A trusted family member, partner, caregiver, or friend may help when:
Anxiety makes it hard to speak
They can describe changes in functioning
They can help with transportation or technology
The clinician may still ask to speak with you privately for part of the appointment.
The support person should not answer every question for you, pressure you, or prevent you from discussing sensitive concerns.
Arrive according to the practice’s instructions
Plan support if driving is difficult
Avoid arriving extremely early if waiting increases anxiety, but allow enough time to check in without rushing.
When driving anxiety is severe, arrange safe transportation rather than placing yourself or others at risk.
Preparing for a Telehealth Anxiety Evaluation
Eligible patients must be physically located in Maryland, Washington, DC, or Virginia during Tinka Health Services telehealth appointments.
Choose a setting where you can speak honestly about:
Telehealth Care for Anxiety in Maryland, DC, and Virginia
What If You Do Not Have Privacy?
Another person is controlling the conversation
You do not feel safe speaking
You are at work or school
You are in a public place
The location changes during the visit
Sitting in a safely parked vehicle
Answering some questions through another approved method
Do not hide a safety concern because someone else is present.
How to reopen the appointment link
What to do if video fails
If the connection ends during a safety assessment, remain available by telephone.
Continue through an approved alternative when appropriate
Direct you to urgent or emergency care
Check Insurance and Cost Questions Before the Visit
Does coverage differ for evaluation and follow-up?
Insurance verification does not guarantee that a claim will be paid.
For a more detailed guide, visit
Insurance and Cost Questions for Anxiety Care
What Should You Bring to the Appointment?
For telehealth, keep these items within reach.
You do not need to bring a perfectly organized folder.
Some questions may feel unrelated to anxiety.
They help distinguish among conditions with overlapping symptoms and identify safety concerns.
Will You Need a Screening Questionnaire?
You may be asked to complete a questionnaire before or during the appointment.
Fear that something bad will happen
Standardized assessment measures can support an initial interview and help track symptoms over time, but they do not replace clinical judgment.
Answer based on your actual recent experience rather than what you think the clinician expects.
A questionnaire score does not independently determine the diagnosis or treatment.
Not every patient needs laboratory testing.
Another medical condition may explain the symptoms
Possible tests depend on the patient’s symptoms, history, and medication.
There is no single laboratory test that confirms an anxiety disorder. Physical examination and testing may instead help identify or rule out other causes.
After gathering the information, the clinician may discuss:
SAMHSA advises leaving outpatient treatment appointments knowing the next appointment date and whether any tasks need to be completed beforehand.
Before the appointment ends, consider asking:
Who should I contact with questions?
What should I do if symptoms worsen?
Will You Receive a Diagnosis at the First Appointment?
A provisional diagnosis may be used when more information is needed.
This does not mean the symptoms are not real or that treatment cannot begin.
Immediate concerns such as sleep, panic, functioning, substance use, or safety may still be addressed.
Common Mistakes to Avoid When Preparing
Trying to Diagnose Yourself Before the Appointment
Learning about anxiety can be useful, but you do not need to decide which disorder you have.
Heart, breathing, digestive, sleep, and neurological symptoms may be important to the evaluation.
Accurate information is necessary for diagnosis, medication safety, and treatment planning.
Minimizing Symptoms Because You Still Function
Work, school, or parenting performance does not show the full emotional and physical cost.
Exaggerating Symptoms to Be Taken Seriously
Clear examples of actual symptoms and impairment are more useful than trying to sound severe.
Independent medication changes may cause withdrawal, worsening symptoms, or diagnostic confusion.
Preparation should make the appointment easier, not become an exhausting anxiety ritual.
Waiting Until Every Record Is Available
Missing documents can often be obtained later. Attend the appointment with what you have.
What If Anxiety Makes It Hard to Speak?
Give the clinician your written summary
Begin with the most important symptom
Ask for a moment to collect your thoughts
Tell the clinician that speaking is difficult
Request written instructions at the end
A useful opening statement may be:
“I am very anxious about this appointment and may have difficulty explaining everything. I wrote down the main concerns.”
The clinician is evaluating the symptoms, not your ability to give a polished presentation.
What If You Cry or Have a Panic Attack?
Crying, trembling, becoming quiet, or experiencing panic during an evaluation does not mean the appointment has failed.
Tell the clinician what you are experiencing.
Help you orient to the room
Severe or unfamiliar chest pain, fainting, major breathing difficulty, or other possible medical emergencies should receive urgent medical assessment.
What If You Forget Something Important?
Contact the practice through its approved communication method when clinically important information was missed.
Less urgent information can often be discussed at follow-up.
“I experience persistent worry and panic while driving.”
“Worry has been present for years. Panic while driving began four months ago.”
Whether thoughts of death, self-harm, or suicide are present
This is enough to begin a meaningful evaluation.
When Not to Wait for the Scheduled Evaluation
Contact a healthcare professional promptly when:
You are no longer sleeping adequately
Work or school attendance is deteriorating
Alcohol or substance use is increasing
A medication change caused severe symptoms
You cannot care safely for dependents
An earlier appointment, medical assessment, medication review, or higher level of care may be needed.
Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room when someone:
May harm themselves or another person
Has a suicide plan and intends to act
Has immediate access to lethal means
Has severe or unfamiliar chest pain
Has sudden weakness or difficulty speaking
Do not wait for an anxiety evaluation, routine appointment, website response, voicemail, email, or patient portal message during an immediate emergency.
Tinka Health Services is not an emergency service.
Common Questions About Preparing for an Anxiety Evaluation
Referral requirements depend on the practice, insurance plan, and type of service. Confirm this before the appointment when possible.
Do I Need to Know Which Anxiety Disorder I Have?
No. The clinician’s role is to evaluate the pattern and consider possible diagnoses.
Should I Stop Caffeine Before the Appointment?
Do not make dramatic changes solely to appear less anxious. Report your normal use accurately. The clinician can discuss whether reduction may be helpful.
Should I Take My Regular Medication?
Follow the prescribing instructions unless a healthcare professional tells you otherwise.
Yes. Notes may help you remember symptoms, medications, questions, and goals.
A trusted person may attend when the practice permits and you consent. The clinician may still request private time with you.
An evaluation does not guarantee a prescription. Recommendations depend on the clinical findings, medical history, preferences, risks, and available treatment options.
Therapy may be recommended depending on the anxiety pattern, severity, functioning, and treatment goals.
Will I Need More Than One Appointment?
Possibly. Some evaluations require additional history, records, medical testing, or follow-up.
